transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-28
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~58m
Attendees: Maya, Gregor (Redwood); Priya, Tom, Liam, Sara (Skyline)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everybody, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on this account. With me is Gregor, our solutions engineer.
[00:12] Priya Natarajan: Hi thanks, yeah, excited to dig in. We wanted to focus on how Redwood would plug into our existing RAG pipeline and what switching to Dedicated or Private would look like from an infra perspective.
[00:25] Gregor Li: Great. Can you give a quick run-down of current stack? SDKs, orchestrator, retriever?
[00:33] Tom Reyes: Sure. We run a Python stack, heavy Lang Chain usage — sorry, LangChain — plus Llama Index for doc ingestion, Vector DB is Pinecone for now. Our orchestrator is Airflow for batch, and a Node-based API for low-latency queries.
[00:47] Gregor Li: Okay, that helps. Two common integration patterns: call Redwood directly from your backend via our SDKs, or sit a gateway/proxy in front for multi-model routing and quota enforcement.
[00:58] Liam O'Connor: Quick question — if we go hosted, how do we handle PII? We need to avoid sending raw PII to third-party unless it's encrypted with our keys.
[01:08] Maya Chen: Totally. For that use-case teams usually pick Dedicated or Private. Private (VPC) gives you a customer-managed control plane and option to integrate with your KMS/HSM. Dedicated gives isolation and predictable throughput; plus we can set retention policies. We'll share the SOC2 + encryption notes.
[01:23] Sara Mendez: Are there restrictions on bringing your own KMS? We use an internal vault and would prefer not to push key material out.
[01:30] Gregor Li: You can bring your KMS keys in Private deployments; for Dedicated we support envelope encryption with customer-managed KMS integrations. There are some config steps for the HSM endpoints but we have a runbook.
[01:41] Priya Natarajan: From an SDK perspective, we have hundreds of call sites. How invasive is the SDK change? Do you have LangChain/LlamaIndex connectors we can drop in?
[01:50] Gregor Li: Yes, we maintain LangChain adapters and a LlamaIndex loader example. They map to our Python SDK and to our Node SDK for streaming. We've found customers replace the transport layer with a short shim — often 4-8 lines to instantiate the Redwood client and feed in the retriever results. I'll share the repo link.
[02:05] Tom Reyes: Is there a sample for token streaming with the Node SDK? We use socket streaming to push partial answers to clients.
[02:12] Gregor Li: Yes, our Node SDK supports streaming and function-calling style patterns. There's a small example in the repo. We'll send a snippet after the call.
[02:20] Liam O'Connor: Okay, gateway patterns — we want rate limiting per team and per-route quotas, with throttling spikes. Is that better handled in our gateway or Redwood?
[02:31] Maya Chen: Two options: 1) do rate-limiting at your gateway and use the Redwood per-route quotas for extra guardrails, or 2) use Redwood as the enforcement point — we support per-token quotas, per-route SLOs, and per-API-key usage caps. Many customers do a hybrid: edge gateway for coarse limits with Redwood enforcing billing-safe quotas.
[02:51] Priya Natarajan: If we let Redwood enforce, does that add latency? We need p95 < 300ms for short prompts.
[02:59] Gregor Li: Minimal. Enforcement is in the control plane; token generation stays on the fast path. For p95 targets we recommend Dedicated with reserved GPUs and our continuous batching tuned. Also we can pin a smaller model variant for low-latency routes.
[03:14] Sara Mendez: Does Redwood support a sidecar model, like an envoy plugin or sidecar container, so we don't modify all of our services?
[03:21] Gregor Li: Yes — we have a sidecar pattern: a small proxy that handles auth, local caching (prefix/K V cache), and batching. It's deployable as a Kubernetes daemonset or as an istio/envoy filter. The sidecar reduces calls to the remote endpoint by serving cached KV responses. Note: transcription sometimes shows K V cache as K V cache, but this is the same as KV cache.
[03:40] Tom Reyes: If we use sidecar, how do we do observability? We need end-to-end traces and token-level cost attribution per user/session.
[03:49] Gregor Li: We export OpenTelemetry spans and metrics. You can tag tokens with session IDs and have token counters emitted. Our Console will break down cost by token, by route and by API key. We also provide logs and a streaming webhook for live events.
[04:02] Liam O'Connor: Any sample dashboards?
[04:05] Maya Chen: We'll share a dashboard template. Also, you can ingest traces into your existing system; we emit Jaeger-compatible traces.
[04:11] Priya Natarajan: About LlamaIndex — our ingestion pipeline uses a custom chunking scheme. Will we need to re-chunk for Redwood?
[04:19] Gregor Li: Not necessarily. LlamaIndex sits upstream; the vector DB content is what matters. If you keep embeddings compatible, everything works. For latency though, smaller chunk sizes can reduce retrieval time but increase tokens during generation — it's a tradeoff. We can run quick tests with your dataset.
[04:36] Tom Reyes: Can we do a pilot with Dedicated capacity for an hour's worth of load testing? We'll want to simulate 200 qps with 250 token avg.
[04:43] Maya Chen: Yes, we can set up a short Dedicated pilot. For 200 QPS at 250 tokens we generally recommend at least X GPUs — we'll size this in the follow-up. I'll attach a quick sizing calc.
[04:58] Priya Natarajan: Pricing question — how is token billing handled with caching? If we cache prefixes or responses, do we still get billed per-token?
[05:07] Gregor Li: Billing is per generated token, but cache hits that avoid generation aren't billed. If you use prefix/KV caching and we return cached text, you won't be charged for that generation. We also support local client-side caching patterns.
[05:20] Priya Natarajan: Nice. Also curious about concurrency and batching. We're thinking of continuous batching but worried about latency spikes.
[05:29] Gregor Li: Continuous batching is workload-aware. For latency-sensitive routes you can set a max batch window (e.g., 5ms) and target small batch sizes. For throughput routes you might accept larger windows. The runtime picks kernels and quantization levels; we can recommend quantized model variants to reduce latency and memory.
[05:47] Liam O'Connor: Security — do you provide audit logs and RBAC that sync to our SSO?
[05:54] Maya Chen: Yes, RBAC plus SSO via SAML/SCIM for user provisioning and audit logs with event retention options. We'll include the security pack PDF.
[06:03] Sara Mendez: What about private deployments on-prem? We have some air-gapped workloads for government clients.
[06:10] Gregor Li: We offer an on-prem package; it's heavier lift but we support air-gapped images and an offline installer plus local telemetry. Generally that's preceded by a discovery and a support contract.
[06:20] Priya Natarajan: For the LangChain connectors, are there examples for retriever/chain outputs mapping to function-calling, structured outputs?
[06:29] Gregor Li: Yes, the LangChain adapter supports streaming LLM outputs and structured function-calling hints. For LlamaIndex we have a loader and a query-time example that shows how to map metadata and function calls.
[06:40] Tom Reyes: Any gotchas around streaming + function calls with our web sockets?
[06:44] Gregor Li: The main things are backpressure semantics and partial outputs. Our SDK exposes events for chunk start/chunk end and error states. In Node we surface an async iterator so you can pipe chunks to your sockets.
[06:56] Liam O'Connor: Competitors — we tested OpenAI's API and saw variance in latency; does Redwood provide any model-variant fallback for outages?
[07:05] Maya Chen: Yes, smart routing allows fallback to compatible model variants and cross-region failover. We have canary and automatic fallback policies.
[07:13] Priya Natarajan: What about per-team quotas? We have multiple product teams sharing the instance.
[07:18] Gregor Li: You can create API keys scoped per team with per-key quotas and per-route SLOs. The Console surfaces per-team cost and usage breakdown.
[07:27] Sara Mendez: Ok, let's talk integration effort. If we adopt sidecar + LangChain adapters, how long is the expected effort?
[07:33] Gregor Li: For a greenfield integration with the adapters and sidecar, teams usually get a POC in 2-3 weeks. If you require Private deployment or custom KMS, it's longer — 6-10 weeks for on-prem.
[07:45] Tom Reyes: We need people assigned for the pilot. Who will lead on Redwood side?
[07:49] Maya Chen: I'll be the AE owner, Gregor will be the SE lead on technical. We can assign a solutions architect if the pilot grows.
[07:57] Priya Natarajan: Can you walk us through a small code example now?
[08:00] Gregor Li: Sure — pseudo: instantiate Redwood client, set retriever results, call generate with streaming callbacks. [short code blurts]...
[08:30] [code readouts] Gregor Li: — and if you want a drop-in for LangChain: from redwood import RedwoodLLM, then wrap in LangChain LLM wrapper, that's it.
[09:00] Liam O'Connor: Any limitations for embeddings? We may migrate away from Pinecone.
[09:06] Gregor Li: We support embeddings via our embeddings endpoint, and you can host your vectors in any DB. We have a managed embed pipeline or you can call and store vectors yourself.
[09:18] Priya Natarajan: For the pilot, we want observability hooks — traces emitted to our OTEL collector and a demo dashboard.
[09:26] Maya Chen: Gregor will share a dashboard and an OTEL config example; we'll also grant temporary Console access.
[09:33] Sara Mendez: Regarding quotas: do you support burst credits, e.g., baseline monthly plus burst?
[09:40] Gregor Li: Yes, Dedicated supports burst pools — you can reserve baseline throughput and allow controlled bursts. We'll include config examples.
[09:48] Tom Reyes: Anything else on compliance? We need to validate data residency in EU for some of our clients.
[09:54] Maya Chen: We have EU regions and can pin routing to region. For Private we can deploy control plane in your region.
[10:02] Priya Natarajan: Alright, wrap up — what do you need from us to start the pilot?
[10:06] Maya Chen: Access to a small sample dataset, expected QPS and latency targets per route, and whoever will be the infra lead to coordinate VPC peering or sidecar rollout.
[10:18] Priya Natarajan: We'll send that. Thanks.
[10:22] [some small crosstalk and 'thanks everyone']

End recap (verbatim notes):
- Redwood to send: security pack (SOC2, network diagram), LangChain/LlamaIndex example repos, Node streaming snippet, dashboard template, Dedicated sizing calc.
- Customer to send: sample dataset, QPS/latency SLOs, infra contact and peering window.
